analysis.one_liner: Bars permits for new coal plants unless they capture 85% of their carbon emissions.
analysis.headline: The bill to block new uncontrolled coal plants died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its referral on March 11, 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop federal and state permitting authorities from issuing Clean Air Act permits for new coal-fired power plants unless the plants capture at least 85% of their carbon dioxide and store it permanently underground [S2][S3]. It would also deny free or below-market pollution allowances to any new coal plant built without that technology under any future climate program [S2][S3]. The restrictions would last until a comprehensive climate program cutting U.S. emissions to 80% below 1990 levels by 2050 took effect [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee on the day it was introduced and never advanced further [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Communities near proposed coal plants, since the bill would prevent construction of new coal plants without carbon capture. Also the general public, which faces the costs of climate change, and competing power sources like renewables and natural gas that would gain relative market position. Existing utilities would gain by avoiding new coal competitors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near proposed coal plants and the public

how_it_helps.text: No new coal plant could get a Clean Air Act permit unless it captured and permanently sequestered at least 85% of its carbon dioxide, meaning plants that simply vented their carbon could not be built [S2][S3].

Any new coal plant built without carbon capture would be barred from receiving free or below-market emission allowances in any future federal climate program, removing the prospect of a windfall [S2][S3].

The moratorium would remain in effect until Congress or the EPA adopted a comprehensive program requiring immediate emission cuts rising to 80% below 1990 levels by 2050, so there would be no gap in protection [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Utilities planning new coal-fired power plants, and coal mining companies that supply them, would bear the cost of building plants with carbon capture technology or forgoing new plants. Electricity customers in utility service territories could face higher rates if carbon capture technology proved expensive. Companies that expected to receive free emission allowances under a future climate program would lose that benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Utilities, coal companies, and possibly electricity customers

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a high bar: capturing 85% of carbon dioxide and permanently sequestering it was not commercially demonstrated at the time, so in practice the bill could have blocked virtually all new coal plant construction, including plants utilities had already invested in planning [S2][S3].

If blocked coal plants are replaced by natural gas plants, that fuel carries its own price volatility and supply risk, and electricity costs could rise in some regions; critics also argued that a national moratorium raises energy reliability concerns [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would substantially reduce future carbon emissions by preventing construction of coal plants without carbon capture, a benefit accruing to the public over decades. The cost falls on utilities and coal companies that would need to adopt expensive, not-yet-commercial technology or cancel projects, with some risk of higher electricity prices. The bill's design is aggressive: it effectively functions as a moratorium on most new coal construction unless carbon capture is proven, which supporters considered necessary and critics considered overreach. There is no record of committee action, so any judgment about its practical effects was never tested in hearings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Moratorium on Uncontrolled Power Plants Act of 2008 on March 11, 2008, joined by Rep. Edward Markey [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction and then to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality [S5].
No further action was recorded on the bill for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Utilities planning new coal-fired plants and coal mining companies, which faced no new permitting restrictions or allowance forfeiture requirements. Environmental groups and communities near proposed plants gained nothing, since the moratorium never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities planning coal plants and coal companies

for.role: Chair, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform; bill sponsor

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no hearing or markup was held [S1][S5].

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: The bill would prevent construction of new coal-fired power plants without carbon capture and deny free emission allowances to plants built without it. The industry's interest in avoiding these restrictions runs against the public's interest in reducing greenhouse gas emissions. No action was taken, so the industry's position was unchanged.

industries.industry: Renewable and natural gas power generators
industries.note: Blocking new coal plants would shift investment toward other electricity sources. Whether this aligns with the public interest depends on cost and reliability outcomes.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and sequestration technology firms
industries.note: The bill's 85% capture requirement could create demand for sequestration technology if viable, but the technology was not commercially demonstrated, so the bill as written could have eliminated new coal construction rather than creating a market for the technology.
